newsitem.title: USA: Soyinka says Nigeria military must pay for "crimes".
newsitem.headline: Soyinka says Nigeria military must pay for "crimes".

text.p: Exiled Nigerian Nobel Prize laureate Wole Soyinka called Nigeria's military regime a "gang of torturers and assassins" on Tuesday and said their crimes should be addressed in the future.
Soyinka, charged with treason in Nigeria, said that the opposition has been considering what to do with the current regime if it ever acquired power in the future.

"The catalogue of crimes being committed against the Nigerian people during the current and preceding insanities of power has to be addressed at some time in the future," said Soyinka, who was awarded the 1986 Nobel Prize for literature.
Soyinka was speaking at Harvard University in the first of three lectures on racial reconciliation, which will form the basis a book.
The radical playwright and novelist who fled to Europe and the United States more than two years ago leads the opposition party National Liberation Party Council of Nigeria (NALICON).

His bestseller, "The Open Sore of a Continent: A Personal Narrative of the Nigerian Crisis," grew out of previous lectures at Harvard and formed a scathing indictment of Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha.

Soyinka and 11 other dissidents were charged with treason last month by the Nigerian government for bombings that killed Nigerian soliders in December. They face the death penalty if convicted. Soyinka has denied involvement.

In his first lecture on Tuesday, entitled "Reparations, Truth and Reconciliation," he said he and other members of the Nigerian opposition have been watching South Africa's truth commissions with an interest in Nigeria's future.
"Will this undertaking truly reconcile the once-warring tribes of our community? My inclination is very much toward the negative prognosis," he told an audience of about 80 students and faculty.

"The Nigerian opposition group to which I belong, with an eye already on the future on the Nigerian nation after the expulsion of the current dictator and his gang of torturers and assassins, decided on a close monitoring of the proceedings with a view to extracting lessons that may be useful on a political dispensation that must replace the present," he said.

Security at the Harvard lecture hall was lax with just one guard present, but tensions rose when two members of the audience, one of whom said Soyinka was a mass murderer, were escorted from the room.

The Harvard series and three recent lectures he gave at Emory College in Atlanta, where Soyinka currently teaches, will form the book "The Burden of Memory, the Muse of Remission," to be released next year by Oxford University Press.
